item.title: Magistrate weighs sentencing options
item.description: A SUSPENDED sentence should not be viewed as an easy way out in domestic violence cases, Magistrate Yogesh Prasad warned as he considered a vegetable seller’s assault on his wife. On August 10, the 36-year-old man admitted in court to assaulting his wife following an argument after they returned from church.
item.content:encoded:
A SUSPENDED sentence should not be viewed as an easy way out in domestic violence cases, Magistrate Yogesh Prasad warned as he considered a vegetable seller’s assault on his wife.

On August 10, the 36-year-old man admitted in court to assaulting his wife following an argument after they returned from church.

The court heard he approached his wife while she was at home with their children and struck her with a stick, causing injuries to the right side of her face and the back of her neck.

The court heard there were financial difficulties in the relationship and that the victim had since moved and was not receiving financial support from the man.

Magistrate Prasad stressed the seriousness of domestic violence and the importance of punishment, noting that offenders could return to similar behaviour.

He said the circumstances of the offending had to be carefully considered and stressed the need to protect victims and ensure offenders understood the seriousness of their conduct.

Sentencing has been scheduled for September 1.

item.title: The Fiji Times corrects Election Date Report
item.description: THE Fiji Times sincerely apologises for an error in our reporting regarding comments made by Minister for Justice and Acting Attorney-General Hon Siromi Turaga on the timing of the next general election. While efforts were made to correctly transcribe the Minister’s remarks, an error occurred in the transcription and subsequent reporting of his comments during an interview on Wednesday this week.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Times sincerely apologises for an error in our reporting regarding comments made by Minister for Justice and Acting Attorney-General Hon Siromi Turaga on the timing of the next general election.

While efforts were made to correctly transcribe the Minister’s remarks, an error occurred in the transcription and subsequent reporting of his comments during an interview on Wednesday this week.

While speaking, Mr Turaga said Government was working towards an election timeline “around December to ….., yeah”.

The transcript incorrectly translated the “December to…” as “December 2”.

When the Leader of the Opposition’s office issued a statement yesterday questioning the A-G for announcing the “election date”, a senior The Fiji Times staff replied to this email and informed the Opposition media liaison officer that the mistake was made by the newspaper – not the A-G.

Despite being informed of the error, the Opposition office released the statement publicly on their Facebook page this morning.

The Fiji Times deeply regrets the error and any confusion or inconvenience it may have caused the Minister, the Prime Minister, the Electoral Management Board, Members of Parliament and the public.

We have taken steps to correct the record in our print and online editions.

We reaffirm our commitment to accuracy, fairness and credibility in our reporting.

item.title: Lawyer seeks documents
item.description: THE lawyer representing former Fiji Corrections Service officer Epeli Laqeni is seeking access to the organisation’s standard operating procedure, arguing it is relevant to his defence. Mr Laqeni, who is alleged to have murdered his de facto partner in Nakasi between September 3 and 5 last year, appeared before Justice Usaia Ratuvili on August 11.
item.content:encoded:
THE lawyer representing former Fiji Corrections Service officer Epeli Laqeni is seeking access to the organisation’s standard operating procedure, arguing it is relevant to his defence.

Mr Laqeni, who is alleged to have murdered his de facto partner in Nakasi between September 3 and 5 last year, appeared before Justice Usaia Ratuvili on August 11.

His lawyer Timoci Varinava told the court the document would assist in showing that his client was not at work on the day after the alleged incident but was instead at a hospital.

The State is opposing the request for the document. The application is scheduled to be heard on September 15.

item.title: Grandpa jailed for rape
item.description: A 65-YEAR-OLD man, who threatened a 13-year-old boy with a cane knife before attempting to rape him, has been jailed for eight years. The man was convicted after trial of attempted rape and sentenced by Justice Lee James Burney at the High Court in Labasa earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
A 65-YEAR-OLD man, who threatened a 13-year-old boy with a cane knife before attempting to rape him, has been jailed for eight years.

The man was convicted after trial of attempted rape and sentenced by Justice Lee James Burney at the High Court in Labasa earlier this month.

The court heard that on May 2, 2025, the boy went with a friend to the man’s home to collect bele.

After sending the friend away, the man told the boy to get vaseline from his bedroom before pushing him onto a bed and threatening to chop him with a cane knife if he did not remain still.

The boy became frightened and wanted to leave. The man threatened the boy not to tell his friend about what had happened.

The judge rejected the man’s age and health as mitigating factors, despite him being 65 and having suffered a heart attack and hearing problems.

Justice Burney said serious sexual offending against children by elderly and infirm men was prevalent and stressed the need to protect children.

He must serve a non-parole period of four years and eight months before he is eligible for parole.

item.title: Partnership improves border surveillance system
item.description: AUSTRALIA will support Fiji in strengthening its border security through the installation of a new border management system under the Vuvale Partnership. Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the initiative was part of Australia’s continued support for Fiji in addressing border security challenges and transnational crime.
item.content:encoded:
AUSTRALIA will support Fiji in strengthening its border security through the installation of a new border management system under the Vuvale Partnership.

Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the initiative was part of Australia’s continued support for Fiji in addressing border security challenges and transnational crime.

Speaking at the official opening of the Nadi International Airport CCTV Capability and Multi-Purpose Room last week, Mr Roberts said two Australian Border Force officers were based in Suva, with another two stationed in Nadi, to support the Fijian Government.

“To me that shows the sort of partnership that we need in order to address the challenges that we are facing together,” he said.

Mr Roberts said Australia was proud to have supported enhanced CCTV capabilities at Nadi International Airport, including the construction of a control room in partnership with the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service (FRCS) and the Australian Border Force.

He described the investment as a practical step towards strengthening Fiji’s border security.

FRCS chief executive officer Udit Singh said the need for stronger border security was becoming increasingly important as the region faced more complex threats, including illicit trafficking, smuggling and transnational organised crime.

“Our success depends on strong collaboration, effective information sharing, and a coordinated approach to border security,” he said.

Mr Singh said the new system would also improve coordination between partner agencies and support more timely decision-making.

“It will enhance our situational awareness, strengthen frontline operations, and improve our ability to identify, assess, and respond to emerging risks.”

item.title: Villages unite for mangrove initiative
item.description: THE communities of Naisisili and Navotua in Nacula district, Yasawa, have joined forces in a mangrove restoration initiative, planting more than 8000 Rhizophora mangroves, known as tiri in iTaukei. The initiative aims to strengthen coastal protection, restore important mangrove habitat and support the communities’ efforts to respond to the impact of climate change.
item.content:encoded:
THE communities of Naisisili and Navotua in Nacula district, Yasawa, have joined forces in a mangrove restoration initiative, planting more than 8000 Rhizophora mangroves, known as tiri in iTaukei.

The initiative aims to strengthen coastal protection, restore important mangrove habitat and support the communities’ efforts to respond to the impact of climate change.

Naisisili Village headman Mavileko Ratulevu highlighted the importance of mangrove restoration.

“Planting mangroves is very helpful,” Mr Ratulevu said.

“Here in Naisisili, there are two areas where mangroves are found, Tukusaga and Mamada.

“In my opinion, planting mangroves helps reduce coastal erosion in our community.”

For Navotua, the restoration initiative builds on previous community efforts to protect and restore mangrove ecosystems.

Kinisimere Mele, who oversees the mangrove nursery at Navotua, said the community was pleased to continue its involvement in mangrove restoration.

“The first-time mangrove restoration took place here in Navotua, it was successful,” Ms Mele said.

“This is the second time we have participated, and we are grateful for this initiative and the opportunity to continue protecting our environment for future generations.”

The initiative was supported by the Hilton Global Foundation, whose support enabled the two communities to continue their mangrove restoration efforts and planted more than 8000 mangroves.

The collaboration demonstrates the important role communities play in protecting and restoring coastal ecosystems. Through locally-led conservation efforts, Naisisili and Navotua are contributing to the protection of their coastlines and the long-term health of marine and coastal environments in the Yasawas.

item.title: Solar cuts fuel use
item.description: KADAVU’S Vunisea power station is saving about $28,000 a month in fuel costs following the commissioning of a solar photovoltaic and battery energy storage system under the LAKARO Project. The project, officially commissioned at Vunisea Government Station last week, has reduced diesel consumption from about 60 drums a month to 20 drums.
item.content:encoded:
KADAVU’S Vunisea power station is saving about $28,000 a month in fuel costs following the commissioning of a solar photovoltaic and battery energy storage system under the LAKARO Project.

The project, officially commissioned at Vunisea Government Station last week, has reduced diesel consumption from about 60 drums a month to 20 drums.

Each drum holds 200 litres, cutting diesel use by about 8000 litres a month and delivering estimated annual savings of $336,000.

Minister for Public Works, Meteorological Services and Transport Ro Filipe Tuisawau said the project was an important investment in Kadavu’s future.

The project was supported by the governments of the United Arab Emirates and New Zealand through a combined funding contribution of $US2.5million, while the Fiji Government contributed $US350,000 and undertook remedial works at all three LAKARO project sites.

item.title: Contracts lapse
item.description: TWO road maintenance contracts in the Northern Division have not been renewed, Infrastructure Minister Ro Filipe Tuisawau has confirmed. Responding to questions on the status of the contracts, Mr Tuisawau confirmed that the contracts were not renewed but could not comment further as decisions concerning the contracts were made by the board of the Fiji Roads Authority (FRA).
item.content:encoded:
TWO road maintenance contracts in the Northern Division have not been renewed, Infrastructure Minister Ro Filipe Tuisawau has confirmed.

Responding to questions on the status of the contracts, Mr Tuisawau confirmed that the contracts were not renewed but could not comment further as decisions concerning the contracts were made by the board of the Fiji Roads Authority (FRA).

The FRA said the contracts were yet to be finalised and the process was still work in progress.

It declined to provide further details on the contractors, directing questions about their contracts to the companies concerned.
